HR@10 against 99 sampled negatives measures success within 100 candidates; it does not establish full-catalog top-10 quality. Krichene and Rendle show sampled ranking metrics can reverse model order even in expectation. Fixed candidates make comparisons reproducible but preserve sampling bias. Therefore, a gain supports the pinned benchmark objective, with no automatic implication for full-catalog recommendations. [On Sampled Metrics](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)

For uncertainty, adapt paired bootstrap resampling: retain each user’s hit indicators for both models, resample the same users for both within each category, and recompute the equally weighted four-category mean difference. Report the difference, its 95% bootstrap interval, and category-level wins/losses. With 200 users/category, one additional hit changes category HR by 0.005 and macro HR by 0.00125. This interval is conditional on fitted models and fixed candidates; it excludes training-seed and candidate-sampling uncertainty. Pairing follows the approach in [Koehn’s bootstrap study](https://aclanthology.org/W04-3250/).

Repeatedly selecting checkpoints and architectures on the same validation users/candidates creates selection optimism; fixing candidates does not prevent adaptive overfitting. An ordinary bootstrap of the selected winner does not correct that selection process. [Cawley and Talbot](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v11/cawley10a.html) document this general problem. Practical inference: a small adaptively selected gain alone provides weak evidence for prioritizing lag gating over depth correction or a separate objective. Within the fixed protocol, use matched ablations, category consistency, and checkpoint-neighborhood stability as supporting diagnostics; retain the prescribed evaluator and reserve claims of generalization for independent held-out evaluation.
